title: Review: Pienaar & Son Tiny Batch Medium Char
summary:
South African whisky has come a long way in recent years, and Pienaar and Son’s Tiny Batch is one of the bottles that has helped put local whisky on the radar, particularly in the main market with fun gifting campaigns and great social media work. Medium Char is part of a two-part release (the other…

The post Review: Pienaar & Son Tiny Batch Medium Char appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
South African whisky has come a long way in recent years, and Pienaar and Son’s Tiny Batch is one of the bottles that has helped put local whisky on the radar, particularly in the main market with fun gifting campaigns and great social media work.

Medium Char is part of a two-part release (the other being Heavy Char) both single grain, single cask whiskies matured in virgin American oak and bottled at 43% abv. Each cask only produces around 550 bottles, so I would have personally preferred to see “Single Cask” on the label, as there isn’t much “batch” about it.

Pienaar & Son Tiny Batch Medium Char Review

The nose is sweet and fairly delicate. Vanilla, honey, and fresh oak come through first, followed by caramel and a distinct grassy note. There’s a touch of coconut and white chocolate. It’s pleasant, although the oak is definitely doing a lot of the talking.

The palate is soft, sweet, and easy-drinking. Again, vanilla, caramel, and toasted oak lead the way, later being met with baking spice and a little pepper. There’s a nice creamy quality to it, but is overall pretty straightforward. At 43% abv, there’s no heat to speak of, although I’d have liked a little more weight and concentration, however I understand the decision to keep the abv on the more accessible side for this one.

The finish is medium-short, with more vanilla and spice. It’s clean and pleasant, but doesn’t exactly hang around.

Overall, I like what Pienaar & Son are doing here, and I think Tiny Batch is an important whisky for South Africa. I can’t say it’s a bottle I’ll show off in my collection, but I don’t think that’s it’s purpose. Rather, it is a very approachable young whisky with a clear identity. The virgin oak gives it plenty of vanilla and sweetness, while the medium char keeps things from getting too heavy. It’s uncomplicated, and while I would love to see what more age and other casks can bring here, it’s clear that the distillers know what they’re doing – they’ve produced a clean and well-made spirit.

For someone wanting to explore South African whisky, it’s a good place to start. For a serious whisky nerd looking for layers of depth, I’d probably reach for something else.

The Heavy Char is an expression I’m excited to compare side-by-side with this – I’m keen to see what some additional oak influence could contribute to the spirit.

86 proof.

B / $51

title: Review: Ardbeg Trudernish 15 Years Old
summary:

Ardbeg Trudernish (TROO-der-nish) is a 15 year old expression designed to add a little more…

The post Review: Ardbeg Trudernish 15 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Unlike most of the new Ardbeg releases we see, today we have the pleasure of introducing not another special edition but a new member of the family that will be permanently available — the first since An Oa in 2017. Ardbeg Trudernish (TROO-der-nish) is a 15 year old expression designed to add a little more age (and a rare age statement) to the core Ardbeg range. Aged in a mix of bourbon, virgin charred oak, and oloroso sherry casks, the name is inspired by an ancient settlement on Islay’s “Enchanted Cape,” where legend has it the water never freezes.

Meanwhile, Ardbeg has rolled out new bottle designs for its entire lineup — though the updates are not extreme.

Our sample bottle of Trudernish was typically tiny, but as always we’ll do our best with review commentary.

Ardbeg Trudernish 15 Years Old Review

Trudernish is designed to be a softer style of whisky, with moderated smokiness from the peat. At first blush that seems not entirely the case, the nose quite bracing with medicinal, smoke-heavy notes, a mix of beach bonfire and iodine, alongside a tenacious aroma of green herbs and a late-game appearance of juniper. A smoldering Dutch process cocoa powder lingers, increasingly visible with time in glass.

On the palate, the smoke hits quickly but dissipates just as fast. I wouldn’t call this whisky “soft” by any measure, but it definitely sees the initially heavy peatiness drop into the background fairly quickly. What emerges from there offers significant complexity, a mix of torched orange peel, smoldering juniper branches, and a hint of grapefruit rind that reminded me of Malort in the best possible way. (I am on record for my love of Malort, and I refuse to apologize.)

The finish sweetens things up nicely: burnt marshmallow, caramel, and sesame oil, which adds a gentle savoriness to the proceedings. All told I thought the journey was on point from start to finish, though a slightly ashy quality on the fade-out made me long for more of those sweeter notes to reappear.

97.6 proof.

A- / $90

title: Review: Edradour 2000 Vintage 18 Years Old Barolo Cask Finish
summary:
Edradour Distillery has never been afraid of doing things a little differently, and I’m always excited by an opportunity to try their bottlings. This 2000 vintage 18-year old Barolo Cask is a particularly interesting example: spending 12 years in ex-bourbon casks before a lengthy six years in Barolo casks. The result is a whisky where…

The post Review: Edradour 2000 Vintage 18 Years Old Barolo Cask Finish appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Edradour Distillery has never been afraid of doing things a little differently, and I’m always excited by an opportunity to try their bottlings. This 2000 vintage 18-year old Barolo Cask is a particularly interesting example: spending 12 years in ex-bourbon casks before a lengthy six years in Barolo casks.

The result is a whisky where the wine influence is substantial without completely overwhelming the underlying distillery character. Bottled at a punchy 56.5% abv, just 578 bottles were produced.

Edradour 2000 Vintage 18 Years Old Barolo Cask Finish Review

The nose is rich and immediately fruity, with red berries, ripe plums, and dark cherries alongside vanilla, honey, and a pleasing nutty note. There is also a slight earthy, almost leathery quality beneath the fruit, giving the nose far more complexity than a simple wine cask sweetness. The alcohol is certainly assertive, but spending some time bonding with it, becomes beautifully integrated.

The palate is powerful and full-bodied. Dark fruit arrives first, with cherries and red berries leading the way, followed by toasted nuts and a touch of dark chocolate. The Barolo influence brings a pleasant combination of fruitiness and tannic dryness, without owerpowering the malt. At 56.5% abv, it definitely isn’t shy, but dilution reveals a more tropical and decadent side.

The long and warming finish is surprisingly dry, with lingering dark fruit, oak spice, and a hint of tobacco. The wine cask leaves its mark right to the end, but there’s enough malt and oak character to keep the finish balanced.

Overall, this is an excellent example of what a long wine cask finish can do when given enough time to integrate. Six years in Barolo is considerably more than the usual finishing period of modern releases, and it shows. Rather than simply adding a layer of red wine quality to the whisky, the cask has become a major player in this dram’s identity.

The high strength is, in my opinion, an added bonus. It’s powerful, concentrated, and distinctly old-school in character, with a kind of complexity that rewards taking your time.

113 proof.

A / $190

title: Review: Highland Park “Between You and I” 2026
summary:
Highland Park’s collaborative “Between You and I” release launched last year with some of the most objectively strange tasting notes I’ve ever encountered — clearly intentionally, though the whisky certainly had some charm to it that you could find without delving into surrealistic commentary about how the whisky sounds. Now, HP is back with a…

The post Review: Highland Park “Between You and I” 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Highland Park’s collaborative “Between You and I” release launched last year with some of the most objectively strange tasting notes I’ve ever encountered — clearly intentionally, though the whisky certainly had some charm to it that you could find without delving into surrealistic commentary about how the whisky sounds.

Now, HP is back with a second edition, this “Between You and I” a 17 year old release that is a collab with New York-based Egyptian artist Laila Gohar, with a slightly more transparent approach. This offering spends 11 years in refill casks before being finished (for 6 years) in “active, unseasoned new American oak casks.”

Also take note that a completely different second version of BY&I called “Between You and I: Journeys” (black box) was released for 2026 exclusively to travel retail. This version is matured in ex-bourbon and new Spanish oak casks. Reviewed here is the much more available global edition (yellow box).

Who is Laila Gohar? Highland Park explains: “Raised in Egypt and based in New York, Laila is that special kind of artist whose work is instantly recognisable. Blending surrealism, humour, elegance and nostalgia, her edible installations turn everyday ingredients into magical, unforgettable experiences. Think Greek sculptures made from creamy butter, or Japanese Zen gardens that are actually chocolate cake.”

We were thrilled to get the chance to taste this collaborative spirit. Thoughts follow.

Highland Park “Between You and I” 17 Years Old 2026 Review

After a handful of lackluster releases, BY&I 2026 is a masterful return to form. I loved just about everything about this whisky, finding it hard to put down from the jump.

The nose enchants with a gentle layer of orange blossom, evident immediately, more blossom than orange and quite delicate in structure. Time in glass helps to concentrate those aromas and infuse them with honey notes, quite enchanting and increasingly citrusy as things develop. Tertiary aromas include a smattering of baking spice and the slightest hint of peat, taking the form of a layer of smoked sea salt.

The palate is equally refreshing, a sweet (but not too sweet) layer of nougat leading the way to flavors of almond cake, studded with sultanas and some chopped dates. The citrus becomes increasingly dominant the longer the whisky sits on the palate, melding with the deep-seeded granary notes to evoke shortbread cookies dipped in Earl Grey tea. From there it’s a quick ride to what emerges as a classic finish, though I would have expected this had some sherry influence had I not been informed otherwise: marzipan and marmalade in roughly equal proportions, settling into a lengthy and soothing vanilla swirl as it sits just about forever in the back of the throat.

If I have any complaint, it’s with Highland Park’s bottle design for this whisky. The ultra-cool box this whisky comes in is clearly designed by an artist. The bottle inside has the distillery’s boring, greige, text-only branding. Come on, HP!

95 proof.

A / $160 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Nagahama Lightly Peated New Make Spirit
summary:
What does whisky taste like before it touches oak? Technically, we shouldn’t even be calling this a whisky. Japan’s Nagahama offers an opportunity to explore the character of their lightly peated new make spirit, stripping away the influence of maturation and puts the distillate itself front and center. What is New Make? New make (or…

The post Review: Nagahama Lightly Peated New Make Spirit appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
What does whisky taste like before it touches oak? Technically, we shouldn’t even be calling this a whisky. Japan’s Nagahama offers an opportunity to explore the character of their lightly peated new make spirit, stripping away the influence of maturation and puts the distillate itself front and center.

What is New Make?

New make (or white dog in the American whisky world) is essentially whisky post-distillation, pre-maturation. The majority of the flavors you find in your glass are a result of maturation and its many variables, however, there are several production choices made before the spirit enters the cask that have an enormous effect on flavor, mouthfeel, texture, and weight.

Nagahama Lightly Peated New Make Review

The nose demonstrates a pronounced malty character, with fresh cereal sweetness and a faint smoky edge. This expression is lightly peated, but does not carry any aggressively medicinal notes. There really isn’t much more to share here, and I’d be lying if I told you I’m picking up loads of flavor here – but that’s exactly the point of this exercise.

At 59% abv, this spirit is to be approached with caution. The absence of maturation brings additional heat to an already-aggressive abv. In terms of flavor, the malt-forward profile is joined by the light smoke we discovered on the nose. On my second taste after dilution, some orchard fruit reveals itself, but without oak to contribute vanilla, tannin, or dried fruit richness, the focus remains firmly on the underlying spirit.

The finish echoes the malty and gently smoky base, with fresh fruit becoming more apparent as the alcohol is brought into balance.

New make isn’t for everyone, but it certainly can be a fascinating to whisky enthusiasts interested in production processes. Without years in a cask to soften the spirit, integrate flavor, extract from the oak, and develop complexity, the distillate has nowhere to hide. This bottle makes me wish it were easier to get hold of new make from well-known distilleries to achieve a deeper understanding of their house style.

This expression also offers a useful opportunity to experience peated spirit before oak reduces some of the impact.

Overall, this is an educational bottle rather than a conventional sipping whisky.

118 proof.

B / $104

title: Review: Blade and Bow Kentucky Straight Bourbon 12 Years Old Solera Reserve
summary:
The Blade and Bow brand, under the oversight of Nicole Austin, recently launched a new expression that’s unlike anything else in its lineup to date. The concept involves multi–vat solera finishing and blending of the outfit’s (new) Stitzel-Weller distillate, the whiskey spending time in a variety of finishing casks that include Cognac, Bordeaux, Moscatel, and…

The post Review: Blade and Bow Kentucky Straight Bourbon 12 Years Old Solera Reserve appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The Blade and Bow brand, under the oversight of Nicole Austin, recently launched a new expression that’s unlike anything else in its lineup to date. The concept involves multi–vat solera finishing and blending of the outfit’s (new) Stitzel-Weller distillate, the whiskey spending time in a variety of finishing casks that include Cognac, Bordeaux, Moscatel, and Port wood. (The standard Blade and Bow expression uses a solera method, but it’s only made with regular bourbon barrels.) Details are scarce on how the solera system works in this release except for the fact that all these finishing vats are “large-format” in size. We also know the whiskey carries a 12 year old age statement, though there are no details on how long any of the solera cycles are.

This offering is a limited release, but it’s one that appears annually (likely with an character that will evolve over time).

Blade and Bow Kentucky Straight Bourbon 12 Years Old Solera Reserve Review

There’s immediate evidence of the wine-soaked wood in this release, hitting promptly on the nose. Sherry is dominant, with a citrusy oloroso bent, undercut with notes of coconut husks, cloves, and dried raisins and figs. If none of that sounds like anything you’ve tasted in the world of bourbon, that’s intentional. While there’s a certain vanilla-caramel character deep in the background here, the wine influence here is utterly dominant. If I nosed this blind and you told me this was an aggressively finished Scotch, I’d believe it.

It isn’t, however, an aggressively finished Scotch, and the palate is where the more traditional bourbonness of the experience starts to reveal itself. While the sherry-driven wine elements hit first, again heavy with a tannic spin on orange oil and well-roasted nuts, the underbelly of vanilla chews and pecan log points squarely to Kentucky.

While there’s no shortage of flavor in this whiskey, it’s not something that  comes across as completely balanced. The sherry notes spin a bit out of control on the oversized finish, the various wine elements evoking a surprising level of tannic bite.

All told it’s quite the ride — and a rare experience compared to what you’re probably used to our of bourbon country.

104 proof.

B+ / $65

At 58% abv, it’s definitely not messing around. Produced at Ben Nevis distillery and sold as a blended malt, Glencoe…

The post Review: MacDonald’s Glencoe Blended Malt 8 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There’s something I really love about whiskies like this. MacDonald’s Glencoe Blended Malt 8 Years Old isn’t trying to be elegant or polished — it’s a big, sherried, cask-strength Highland blend with plenty of personality.

At 58% abv, it’s definitely not messing around. Produced at Ben Nevis distillery and sold as a blended malt, Glencoe combines Ben Nevis with another undisclosed Highland malt. It carries an age statement of 8 years, but offers more muscle than many others in its age group. This whisky leans heavily into sherry, with a distinctly old-school character that isn’t afraid of some roughness around the edges – something I’m growing particularly fond of.

MacDonald’s Glencoe Blended Malt 8 Years Old Review

The nose is big and immediately heavily sherried, with raisins, dark cherries, and orange peel followed by toffee, toasted nuts, and vanilla. There is an earthy, almost rubbery quality playing in the back, alongside pepper, clove, and a faint mineral note. It’s not conventionally pretty, but that’s kind of why this is an interesting bottle.

The palate is where Glencoe really earns its keep. Rich, oily, and powerful, with dark dried fruit, plum, raisin, and orange giving way to malt, chocolate, pepper, and toasted oak. At 58%, there’s plenty of heat on offer, but loads of flavor to back it up. A slight earthy, savory character keeps the sweetness in check, while a touch of mint and gentle smoke appear with time.

A little dilution softens the alcohol and brings forward some honey, nuts, and citrus. The finish is long, warm, and spicy. A flavor bomb of coffee, dark chocolate, oak, and dried fruit hand around, leaving a pleasantly drying and slightly bitter finish.

There’s a muscular, earthy quality that feels increasingly unusual in modern Scotch. The combination of young whisky, heavy sherry influence and cask-strength bottling produces something that is occasionally unruly but rarely boring. It has plenty of fruit and sweetness, but the darker, dirtier notes that make older styles of Highland whiskies so interesting.

At 8 years old, it’s remarkable how much character this whisky carries. It won’t appeal to anyone looking for a soft, polished dram, but if you enjoy full-bodied heavy whiskies, this is a seriously fun bottle.

116 proof.

A / $55

title: Review: Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon
summary:
This newest expression in Old Forester’s 117 Series almost slipped by us. Crafted entirely at Old Forester’s Main Street Louisville location, it’s a boldly experimental offering called Triple Char. As the name suggests, it’s made using barrels charred for three times the usual length of time than Old Forester normally uses. OldFo typically uses a…

The post Review: Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This newest expression in Old Forester’s 117 Series almost slipped by us. Crafted entirely at Old Forester’s Main Street Louisville location, it’s a boldly experimental offering called Triple Char. As the name suggests, it’s made using barrels charred for three times the usual length of time than Old Forester normally uses. OldFo typically uses a Level 4 char — about 55 seconds of char time, which means the barrels used here spend nearly 3 minutes exposed to open flame. This equates to roughly a char Level 7, something we’ve seen in a couple of other experimental offerings.

Let’s give it a spin.

Old Forester The 117 Series – Triple Char Bourbon Review

Surprisingly, the nose of this ambitious spirit evokes far more than charred wood. Notes of mint and cherry are quite prominent, backed with a heavy chocolate and ground coffee character. There’s plenty of that charry, almost smoky oak in attendance, but the surfeit of additional flavors in the mix helps the whiskey exude aromatic complexity.

The palate keeps all of this rolling right along. Big, burnt caramel flavors lead to layers of coconut and banana, then baked green apples. Quite nutty as it develops, the whiskey quickly navigates its way into a vein of baking spice, big with cloves and a punch of toasted, ground ginger. Above all this bourbon is intense. That may be the amplifying effect of the ultra-torched oak staves — or the oak in combination with the high abv — but the whole affair comes to a head on the in-your-face finish, which is tart and tannic in equal proportions. Time in glass turns things into a real vanilla bomb, though greener herbs, namely bay leaf, always linger in the background.

These ultra-charred releases are always worth investigating to help understand the power of heavily charred oak. If you find it at the distillery, it’s a sample worth picking up.

115 proof.

A- / $65 (375ml)

title: Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey
summary:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement. Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey Review The nose is soft…

The post Review: Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Named after the year the Dunvile’s story began, 1808 is an Irish whiskey blend combining malt, grain, and pot still whiskies. This particular expression was first released in 2021 when the distillery expanded its core range, and is bottled at 40% with no age statement.

Dunville’s 1808 Blended Irish Whiskey Review

The nose is soft and fairly straightforward. Vanilla, green apple, pear, and lemon peel are the main players, with some sweet maltiness sitting underneath, alongside a faint hint of smoke. So far, it’s a pleasant enough dram, but don’t expect layers of complexity.

The palate carries a creamy mouthfeel and is fairly easy-drinking, with lemon, orange, vanilla leading the way. There’s a slight peppery spice and a little char towards the back. The texture is decent, but it does feel a little thin once you start looking for more depth.

The medium-short finish features sweet spice, citrus, and a faint smoky note. Nothing unpleasant, but it disappears fairly quickly.

Overall, this whiskey is fresh, uncomplicated, and a great beginner’s dram. The combination of citrus, orchard fruit, vanilla, and that tiny bit of smoke makes it more interesting than your typical entry-level blend, but there’s certainly not enough weight or complexity here for me to call it an exceptional whiskey – and that’s fine, because it’s not trying to be one.

Where it works really well is as a casual pour or in a cocktail. It’s approachable enough for someone who’s new to whiskey, while still having enough character to stop it being completely forgettable.

Would I choose it over something more serious in the Dunville’s range? No, but again, that’s not what 1808 is trying to accomplish. Either way, my bottle will stay on my shelf and I’m sure the occasion for it will come around. An uncomplicated Irish blend — sometimes it’s exactly what you need!

80 proof.

C / $31

title: Review: Green Spot Quails’ Gate
summary:
We’ve covered almost all the Spot whiskeys over the years, but one pesky limited edition has eluded us. Until now. Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on…

The post Review: Green Spot Quails’ Gate appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve covered almost all the Spot whiskeys over the years, but one pesky limited edition has eluded us. Until now. Green Spot Quails’ Gate is the latest in a trifecta of special Green Spot single pot still Irish whiskeys from Midleton Distillery that crossed the pond back in 2023. First, there’s some back story on this series that we may have not yet shared. The unusually named Wine Geese Series in the Spot portfolio celebrates the Irish diaspora, particularly the so-called “wine geese,” Irish families who left Ireland in the early 1700s and established world-class wineries across the globe.

The first release took us to Bordeaux, the second to Napa, and this latest offering hails from a slightly more obscure wine region, British Columbia. Specifically, the winemaker Quails’ Gate which sits in the Okanagan Valley and has a reputation for fantastic Pinot Noir. Like the two other Wine Geese releases before it, this whiskey begins life as classic Green Spot aged in a mix of bourbon and sherry casks before an unspecified finishing in Quails’ Gate Pinot Noir casks. Thoughts follow.

Green Spot Quails’ Gate Review

Like the other two releases in this series, Quails’ Gate manages to offer a nuanced riff on the flagship Spot while still remaining true to the classic pot still whiskey at its core. The nose kicks off with that familiar, funky pot still spice, some barley sugar, and budding notes of banana bread and split vanilla bean. The finishing cask is nicely integrated into the aroma, delivering undertones of raspberry jam and currants that become richer blackberry cobbler as things open in the glass.

The palate showcases early notes of lemon custard and toffee that are balanced and almost buttery in texture. The tannins from the Pinot cask have reined in some of the more traditional Green Spot sweetness, adding a bit of structure and grip along with woody spices and silky notes of black cherry and orange marmalade. The finish is warm and well-spiced with clove and ginger and lingering notes of Linzer cookies and vanilla pudding. Another golden egg, if you will, from the Wine Geese Series.

92 proof.

A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
